evals.name: build-framework-service-business
evals.prompt: I run a 2-person junk removal outfit in Sacramento — me and my brother-in-law, one truck, about $8k/month revenue, almost all of it from Google Local Services ads that keep getting more expensive every quarter. I don't want another list of marketing tactics. I want an actual method for the next 12 months that I can keep coming back to when things go sideways. Where do I even start?
evals.expected_output: A Five Rings Scroll grounded in this specific business: honest one-line definition, verifiable win condition, real inventory of timber (two people, one truck, LSA dependency), a drilled operating form with cadence, a named opponent and chosen initiative with 2-3 concrete tactics, a survey of how other haulers compete, named unknowns, and a short custom Dokkodo. Should NOT be a generic marketing tactic list or a tour of the whole tactic catalogue.
assertions: Covers all five rings as distinct sections (Earth, Water, Fire, Wind, Void)
States a win condition that a third party could verify (has a number or a date)
Grounds the plan in the user's stated facts: two people, one truck, ~$8k/month, Google LSA dependency
Fire section names a specific opponent rather than leaving it abstract
Declares which of the three initiatives (ken no sen / tai no sen / tai tai no sen) applies, and why
Uses at most three named Fire-book tactics (does not tour the catalogue)
Every named tactic is cashed out into a concrete move, not left as a metaphor
Water section gives a training cadence (daily/weekly/per-cycle), not just goals
Wind section characterizes at least two rival approaches concretely
Void section names at least one specific unknown and one thing the user is pretending to know
Ends with a custom Dokkodo of 3-7 terse precepts specific to this business
Contains no fabricated direct quotations attributed to Musashi
No samurai cosplay: no pseudo-archaic voice, invented Japanese, or closing haiku

evals.name: stress-test-q3-plan
evals.prompt: musashi this — here's the Q3 plan for the dev tools startup I co-founded. We're 6 people, $40k MRR, selling a CI observability tool. Plan: (1) ship the 4 big features customers keep asking for, (2) double content output to 8 blog posts a month, (3) hire 2 AEs to go upmarket into enterprise, (4) match Datadog's pricing on the entry tier so we stop losing deals on price, (5) rebrand with a new logo and site in September. We think if we execute all 5 we hit $100k MRR by year end.
evals.expected_output: A blunt ring-by-ring assessment quoting the actual plan items, with a verdict per ring, the weakest ring named plainly with 2-3 fixes, and a closing verdict. Should catch specifics: matching Datadog on price is fighting on ground the giant chose; 5 simultaneous initiatives with 6 people is a foundation problem; the rebrand is ornament; no named opponent-response; no initiative declared.
assertions: Gives an explicit verdict for each of the five rings (sound / thin / hollow or equivalent)
Cites specific items from the user's five-point plan as evidence, not generic critique
Names one weakest ring plainly
Identifies matching Datadog's entry-tier price as fighting on ground chosen by a stronger opponent
Flags at least one plan item as ornament rather than function (e.g. the September rebrand)
Challenges the feasibility of five simultaneous initiatives for a six-person team
Gives 2-3 concrete fixes for the weakest ring
Closes with a blunt verdict rather than a balanced both-sides summary
Contains no fabricated direct quotations attributed to Musashi
No samurai cosplay: no pseudo-archaic voice, invented Japanese, or closing haiku

evals.name: study-fire-book-applied
evals.prompt: I keep seeing people quote the Book of Five Rings but I've never actually read it. What's the Fire book actually about, and what does 'the body of a rock' mean? Also — is any of it useful for what I'm dealing with, which is a competitor who just launched a near-identical product at 40% of our price and is undercutting us at every renewal?
evals.expected_output: Accurate teaching of the Fire book (position, the three sen, the named tactics) and of iwao no mi, followed by concrete application to the price-undercutting situation — likely release four hands, injure the corners, become the enemy, mountain-sea change. No fabricated quotations. Should not stay in 17th-century Japan.
assertions: Explains the Fire book accurately as being about engagement: position, timing, and initiative
Explains the three sen (ken no sen / tai no sen / tai tai no sen)
Explains 'body of a rock' (iwao no mi) as immovable spirit arising from mastery, and places it correctly as the closing teaching of the Fire book
Applies at least two named Fire-book tactics to the price-undercutting situation with concrete moves
Does not attribute Sun Tzu or Hagakure material to Musashi
Contains no fabricated direct quotations attributed to Musashi
Answers the user's actual competitive problem rather than staying in 17th-century Japan
No samurai cosplay: no pseudo-archaic voice, invented Japanese, or closing haiku
